A dispute of a trivial nature between a landlord and now his transferees and the tenant is awaiting disposal for over 3 decades thanks to the literal and unimaginative approach to the provisions of a procedural statute which times without number has been described as one for advancing justice and not to make a mockery of it.
IK-1954254:L53
2. A bungalow with an attached cottage situated at No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi was taken on lease by one E. B. Brook and he inducted the appellant as a sub-tenant in the cottage portion which may herein after be referred to as demised premises. Mr. Brook surrendered his tenancy and vacated the portion in his actual possession on April 1, 1955 simultaneously calling upon the appellant to hand over possession of premises in his possession to the then landlord one Lakhmir Singh, who is no more.
IK-1954254:L54
Appellant did not vacate the premises in his possession but reached an agreement with Lakhmir Singh, the then landlord on June 20/22, 1955 to become the direct tenant of the then landlord of the premises in his possession on a monthly rent of Rs. 277.50 p. as stated in plaint, effective from May 1,1955.
IK-1954254:L55
On October 10, 1955 appellant filed a petition in the Court of Senior Sub Judge, Delhi under cite11†Section 8 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 ('Act' for short) praying for determination of the standard rent of the premises effective from the date of the commencement of his tenancy. Landlord Lakhmir Singh entered appearance and contested the application inter-alia contending that the petition was barred by limitation.
IK-1954254:L56
The trial court held that the petition was not barred by limitation and fixed the standard rent at Rs. 855/- p.a. with effect from October 1, 1955. This decision was rendered on Aug. 4, 1960.In the meantime, landlord Lakhmir Singh sold the whole bungalow including the demised premises by a deed of conveyance dated December 21, 1959 in favour of respondents Nos. 2 and 3 who on their own were impleaded in the proceedings.
IK-1954254:L57
3. The original landlord Lakhmir Singh and the two transferees from Lakhmir Singh preferred an appeal against the order of the learned Single Judge determining the standard rent: in the court of the District Judge, Delhi. The learned District Judge was of the opinion that in view of the provision contained in cite12†Section 11(b) the petition filed by the appellant for fixation of standard rent was barred by limitation. Accordingly the appeal was allowed and the petition of the appellant was dismissed.
IK-1954254:L58
4. The appellant preferred Civil Revision No. 335-D of 1961 in the High Court the order of Punjab at Chandigarh against of the learned District Judge. A learned Judge of the High Court agreed with the view taken by the learned District Judge that the petition was barred by limitation and accordingly rejected the civil revision petition by his judgment and order dated December 17, 1962 against which the appellant has preferred Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971 by special leave.
IK-1954254:L59
5. During the pendency of the proceedings for determination of standard rent in the trial court, the then landlord Likhmir Singh filed Civil Suit No. 231/56 in the Court of the Senior Sub Judge, at Delhi on July 3, 1956 against the appellant for recovering the arrears of rent and possession. Eviction was sought under cite13†Section 13(1)(a) of the Act primarily on the ground of default in payment of rent despite notice dated May 10, 1956 having been duly served upon the tenant.
IK-1954254:L60
The appellant as defendant contested the suit inter-alia contending that his petition for fixation of standard rent under cite11†Section 8 of the Act has already been instituted and is pending and unless the standard rent is determined he is not in a position to meet the demand of arrears of rent claimed at the agreed rate.
IK-1954254:L61
It was also contended that a suitable reply stating the afore-mentioned facts to the notice served by the landlord was sent yet he has unnecessarily rushed to the Court without waiting for the determination of standard rent. It appears that alongwith filing of the written statement, the appellant-tenant deposited all the arrears of rent as claimed by the plaintiff-landlord. The then landlord made an application on August 1, 1956 for permission to withdraw the amount of rent deposited by the tenant.
IK-1954254:L62
This application of the landlord was resisted on the ground that the amount has been deposited under protest and the landlord could not be permitted to withdraw the same till the standard rent is determined. The application was set down for hearing on October 1, 1956. In the meantime on August 27, 1956 the landlord filed an application under cite14†Section 13(5) of the Act for a direction that the tenant i should deposit the rent as it falls due month by month.
IK-1954254:L63
The order sheet shows that the Court directed notice of the application to be served upon the tenant and be fixed for hearing on October 1, 1956. It appears that the application for withdrawal of the rent deposited by the tenant was heard on October 1, 1956. On October 5, 1956, '. the appellant tenant moved an application under cite15†Section 9 of the Act for fixing interim rent pending the determination of the standard rent of the premises.
IK-1954254:L64
The order sheet shows that the application was set down for hearing on the same day in the afternoon and it was as a matter of fact heard and adjourned for order to October 5, 1956 in the afternoon. An order purports to have been passed on October 6, 1956 to the effect that the Court directed the tenant to deposit future rent at the agreed rate of rent. The appellant contended that what appears to be the order dated October 6, 1956 is a subsequently interpolated writing and no such order was made.
IK-1954254:L65
It is not necessary to refer to the unsavoury details of this allegation save and except that the two learned Judges of the High Court before whom this matter reached at different stages: Justice Tek Chand and Justice D. Falshaw,; both were satisfied that the trial court appeared to be guilty of interpolation and this finding resulted in withdrawal and transfer of the suit pending before the learned Judge to another Court competent to try the same.

Therefore the expression within 6 months from the date on which it is so let'can mean only, let to that tenant who disputes or desires to dispute the standard rent and move the court for determination of standard rent. The language of Clause (b) is simple and unambiguous. 22 At this stage it is better to turn to the scheme of the Act. cite20†Section 13 protects a tenant against eviction: It starts with a non-obstante clause and provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or any contract, no decree or order for the recovery of possession of any promises shall be passed by any court in favour of the landlord against the tenant unless the case is brought within one of the enabling provisions set out in the section.
IK-1954254:L134
One such situation is that the tenant has neither paid nor tendered whole of the arrears of rent within one month of the date on which notice of demand for the arrears of rent has been served on him by the landlord in manner provided in cite21†Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. cite11†Section 8 provides for determination of standard rent.
IK-1954254:L135
cite22†Section 4 clearly places an embargo on the right of the landlord to recover as and by any of rent anything in excess of the standard rent, or any lawful increase that may be claimed in it.
IK-1954254:L136
cite22†Section 4 provides that no tenant shall notwithstanding any agreement to the 1 contrary be liable to pay to his landlord for the occupation of any premises any amount in excess of the standard rent of the premises unless such amount is a lawful increase of the standard rent in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
IK-1954254:L137
Sub-cite23†section 2 provides that any agreement for any payment of rent in excess of the standard rent shall 1 be null and void and shall be construed as if it was an agreement for payment of the standard rent only. Therefore it is indisputable that the tenant is under an obligation to pay standard rent or lawful increase that may be made to it.
IK-1954254:L138
Now where the landlord demands rent at the contractual rate and the tenant has moved a petition for 1 fixation of standard rent how is the tenant to be relieved from the obligation to deposit the agreed rent till the petition for standard rent is decided. To make the scheme of the law effective where the tenant has moved a petition for determination of standard rent, the court must decide it as and by way of a preliminary issue.
IK-1954254:L139
Assuming it is not possible to determine the standard rent as and by way of preliminary issue, the Legislature has taken care to provide for interim arrangement.
IK-1954254:L140
cite15†Section 9 provides that if an application for fixing the standard rent or for determining lawful increase to standard rent is made under cite11†Section 8 , the Court shall as expeditiously as possible make an order specifying the amount or the lawful increase to be paid by the tenant to the landlord pending the final decision of the application and shall appoint a date from which the rent or lawful increase so specified shall be deemed to have effect.
IK-1954254:L141
In this case, the tenant did make an application for fixing the interim rent on Oct. 5, 1956 pen- '. ding the determination of the standard rent in the petition moved by him The order found to be interpolated and hence illegal directed the tenant with effect from October 6, 1956 to pay interim rent at the agreed rate of rent. This order specifying interim rent is found to be interpolated and hence a nullity not binding on the tenant.
IK-1954254:L142
And it is the failure of the tenant to comply with this nullity which has resulted in his defence being struck off. The learned Judge declined to interfere with such an order.
IK-1954254:L143
23 Where the law enables the tenant to move a petition for determination of standard rent and further confers power on the court to determine interim rent so as to enable the tenant to deposit the future rent the failure of the court to give appropriate directions in this behalf would work serious hardship to the tenant more so where the landlord has already filed a suit for eviction on the ground of default in payment of rent.
IK-1954254:L144
In such a situation to give effect to the purpose and object of the Act, the appropriate thing to do would be either to take up the petition for determining the standard rent as a preliminary issue or if it is not possible the court should determine the interim rent fixing a date by which the tenant should deposit the rent in arrears and I direction be given to deposit the future rent at the rate at which interim rent is determined.
IK-1954254:L145
Till these steps are taken and non compliance alleged it would not be open to the court to pass a decree for eviction on the short ground of default in payment of rent. This Legislative scheme clearly emerges from the provisions of the Act and no precedent is necessary to substantiate it. However this Court in cite24†Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v.
IK-1954254:L146
Haji Gulamnabi Haji Sqfibhai after examining the scheme of cite25†Section 12 of the Bombay Rents House and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 which is in pari materia with the scheme of the Act held that where a dispute as to the standard rent is raised and a petition has been filed for determination of the standard rent, and the landlord initiates action for eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent, the court should on the application of the tenant take up the dispute as to standard rent in the first instance and having fixed the standard rent call upon the tenant to pay or tender such standard rent so fixed, on or before a date fixed.
IK-1954254:L147
If the tenant pays the standard rent fixed, on or before the date specified, and continues to pay or tender it regularly till the suit is finally decided, he qualifies for the protection of the Act.
IK-1954254:L148

records.text: The principal dispute concerns O. P. Kathpalia's tenancy and continued possession of the cottage attached to the bungalow at No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi. E. B. Brook originally leased the bungalow and inducted Kathpalia as a subtenant of the cottage. After Brook surrendered his tenancy, the original landlord, Lakhmir Singh, accepted Kathpalia as his direct tenant effective May 1, 1955. Lakhmir Singh subsequently transferred the entire property to respondents Nos. 2 and 3, who became the real contesting respondents. The litigation concerned the timeliness and determination of standard rent, the landlord's claim for arrears and possession, the validity of an alleged future-rent deposit direction, and the tenant's right to defend the possession suit.
records.stage: Overall tenancy, standard-rent and possession litigation

records.text: Brook inducted Kathpalia as a subtenant of the cottage on September 1, 1954, after commencement of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952. Brook surrendered his head tenancy on April 1, 1955, but Kathpalia remained in possession. By an agreement reached in June 1955, Lakhmir Singh accepted Kathpalia as a direct tenant effective May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court treated this subsequent direct tenancy as the relevant letting for the limitation dispute.
records.stage: Tenancy formation and classification for Section 11(b)

records.text: Under Section 11(b), as construed and adopted by the Supreme Court, the six-month period for a standard-rent application concerning premises let after commencement of the Act runs from the commencement of the relevant letting to the particular applicant tenant. It does not necessarily run from the first-ever letting of the premises or from an earlier subtenancy that preceded recognition of the applicant's direct tenancy. The Court reasoned that the contrary construction would prevent subsequent tenants from challenging unreasonable rent and frustrate the protective purpose of the legislation.
records.stage: Supreme Court review of Section 11(b) limitation

records.text: The Supreme Court distinguished Kathpalia's earlier post-Act subtenancy from his subsequently recognized direct tenancy. It observed that the record contained no evidence establishing that Lakhmir Singh had given written consent to Brook's induction of Kathpalia as subtenant. In discussing Sections 2(j) and 13(1)(b), the Court explained the statutory significance of unauthorized post-Act subletting, but did not finally adjudicate a separate eviction claim based on unlawful subletting. The absence of evidence of written consent is an evidentiary assessment, not independent proof that consent could never have existed.
records.stage: Classification of post-Act subtenancy and direct tenancy

records.text: Kathpalia filed his Section 8 application for determination of standard rent in October 1955. The judgment records October 10, 1955 in its factual chronology but also reproduces October 1, 1955 when describing the trial court's reasoning. Both stated dates fall within six calendar months of the direct tenancy's effective commencement on May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court expressly held that the application was within time. This statement reports the Court's adopted conclusion; the conflicting filing-date references are not resolved into a single verified date.
records.stage: Section 8 application and Supreme Court limitation review

records.text: The District Judge rejected Kathpalia's standard-rent application as time-barred by treating his September 1, 1954 induction as Brook's subtenant, or the earlier letting of the premises, as controlling the limitation period despite his subsequent direct tenancy effective May 1, 1955. The Punjab High Court substantially adopted that interpretation. The Supreme Court expressly rejected their construction of Section 11(b), holding that limitation must be assessed by reference to the relevant letting to the applicant tenant. The lower-court construction is reported solely as a rejected contrary position and is not an operative legal premise.
records.stage: District Judge appeal, High Court revision and Supreme Court limitation review

records.text: On August 4, 1960, the trial court held Kathpalia's standard-rent application timely and fixed standard rent at Rs. 855 per annum. The District Judge allowed the landlord-side appeal on limitation grounds without deciding the proper amount, and the High Court upheld that limitation approach. Because the amount had not been examined by those appellate courts, the Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971, set aside the adverse limitation decisions, and remitted the landlord's appeal to the District Judge for determination of the proper standard rent. The Supreme Court did not finally fix or affirm Rs. 855 per annum as the operative standard rent.
records.stage: Standard-rent determination, Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971

records.text: Lakhmir Singh commenced Civil Suit No. 231/56 on July 3, 1956, seeking recovery of rent arrears and possession under Section 13(1)(a), alleging default despite a demand notice dated May 10, 1956. Kathpalia disputed the claim, explaining that his standard-rent application was pending and that the claimed arrears were calculated at the disputed contractual rate. The landlord's pleaded nonpayment allegation is not equivalent to a judicial determination that every statutory condition for eviction was satisfied.
records.stage: Trial court rent recovery and possession suit

records.text: Kathpalia deposited the arrears of rent claimed by Lakhmir Singh during the trial proceedings, under protest and while maintaining his challenge to the contractual rate. The Supreme Court noted that the claimed arrears had been deposited at the first hearing. This is an actual historical deposit of previously claimed arrears; it does not establish payment of subsequently accruing future rent, compliance with any later valid interim-rent determination, or satisfaction of the separate one-month statutory payment-or-tender condition following a qualifying demand notice.
records.stage: Eviction suit and Section 13(1)(a) payment dispute

records.text: Lakhmir Singh applied on August 1, 1956 for permission to withdraw the arrears deposited by Kathpalia and separately applied on August 27, 1956 under Section 13(5) for directions requiring future rent to be deposited month by month. Kathpalia opposed withdrawal before standard rent had been determined and sought interim-rent determination under Section 9 on October 5, 1956. These applications were procedural requests by the respective parties. Filing them did not itself establish an effective future-rent deposit order or actual payment under such an order.
records.stage: Trial suit rent applications and Section 9 interim-rent request

records.text: The Supreme Court adopted the statutory reasoning that Section 13 protects a tenant against recovery of possession unless an applicable statutory enabling ground is established. Section 4 prevents recovery of rent exceeding standard rent or a lawful increase. Where a standard-rent petition remains pending during an eviction suit based on nonpayment, the trial court should determine standard rent as a preliminary issue or, if that is not practicable, determine interim rent under Section 9 and specify appropriate payment dates and future deposit requirements. An eviction consequence cannot properly rest merely on alleged noncompliance before the required valid determination and directions have been made.
records.stage: Supreme Court review of eviction protection and interim rent

records.text: In the earlier proceedings, the landlord relied on a purported order dated October 6, 1956 directing Kathpalia to deposit future rent at the agreed monthly rate. The trial court subsequently struck off Kathpalia's defence on the asserted ground of noncompliance with that direction. The High Court declined relief against the sanction despite having identified serious interpolation in the order record. This describes the historical position adopted in the lower proceedings; it does not establish that the purported direction was genuinely made or legally binding.
records.stage: Trial court defence sanction and High Court revisions

records.text: The original trial record concerning the purported October 6, 1956 rent direction displayed suspicious alterations. Justice Falshaw of the Punjab High Court ordered transfer of the pending proceedings to another competent trial court on August 20, 1957, and Justice Tek Chand subsequently confirmed the concern about interpolation. The Supreme Court adopted the conclusion that the purported rent direction was interpolated, legally nonexistent and incapable of binding Kathpalia. The precise date on which the record was altered was not established.
records.stage: High Court transfer proceedings and Supreme Court review of interpolated order

records.text: Because the purported future-rent direction was a legal nullity, the Supreme Court held that failure to comply with it could not justify striking off Kathpalia's defence under Section 13(5). The Court set aside the interpolated order dated October 6, 1956 and the order striking off the defence, and held that Kathpalia must be permitted to defend the possession suit on its merits. This restores procedural protection and an opportunity to contest eviction; it is not a final adjudication that Kathpalia has an unconditional or permanent right to possession.
records.stage: Civil Appeals Nos. 465 and 466 of 1971, defence sanction review

records.text: The landlord's suit had been dismissed for default on December 12, 1956 and restored on December 30, 1957. Kathpalia appealed on January 2, 1958 and sought condonation of delay. His assertion that the challenged orders had been made without communication to him was presented in the condonation application, not independently established as an exact notification history. The Supreme Court found sufficient cause for condonation in the procedural chronology, the uncertain timing of the interpolated order and the serious injustice arising from loss of the statutory defence. It set aside the refusal to condone delay and the related High Court orders.
records.stage: Miscellaneous civil appeal, High Court revisions and Supreme Court delay review

records.text: The Supreme Court referred to its earlier decision in Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Sqfibhai as support for the comparable statutory rent-protection scheme. The cited passage states a conditional sequence: the court first determines standard rent and fixes a date for payment or tender; if the tenant pays or tenders the fixed amount by that date and continues regular payment or tender until final disposition, statutory protection may follow. These are legal conditions drawn from the reported precedent. The passage does not establish that Kathpalia had already fulfilled those conditions or paid future rent.
records.stage: Analogous precedent discussed during interim-rent and eviction review

records.text: For Kathpalia's own proceedings, the Supreme Court directed that the trial court first decide the outstanding Section 9 interim-rent application and then call upon the tenant to deposit arrears calculated at the interim rate determined. The District Judge was separately to determine the proper standard rent on remand and call upon the tenant to make good the deposit in accordance with that determination. These are directions establishing a future process and conditional payment obligations; the judgment does not state that those subsequently required payments had already been made.
records.stage: Remand directions for interim rent and standard rent

records.text: The Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971 and remitted the landlord's appeal against the trial court's standard-rent determination to the District Judge, Delhi, for consideration of the proper amount. Separately, it allowed Civil Appeals Nos. 465 and 466 of 1971 and remitted the proceedings concerning interim rent, rent recovery and possession to the trial court for further adjudication on their merits, with Kathpalia's defence restored. The two remands have different receiving courts and different issues. Neither remand constitutes a final determination of the standard-rent amount, an adjudication that all future rent was paid, or a final decision awarding permanent possession to either side.
records.stage: Final appellate orders and remand scope

records.text: The judgment contains inconsistent statements about the monthly contractual rent. Its initial account reports Rs. 277.50 per month as stated in the plaint, while its later account of the direct tenancy reports Rs. 269.50 per month and a payment of Rs. 539 for May and June 1955. The earlier purported future-rent order is described using Rs. 277.50. These statements should not be silently reconciled into a single verified contractual amount. The Rs. 855 annual standard rent was fixed at trial level but remained subject to the remitted landlord appeal.
records.stage: Direct tenancy, contractual rent and standard-rent appeal

records.text: The judgment expressly identifies October 10, 1955 as the filing date of Kathpalia's standard-rent application in its factual chronology, but reproduces October 1, 1955 in passages describing the trial court's and District Judge's limitation reasoning. The source does not resolve this discrepancy. The Supreme Court's conclusion that the application was timely is a reported judicial holding; the statement pack does not replace the conflicting date references with an independently verified single filing date.
records.stage: Standard-rent petition and limitation review

records.text: Lakhmir Singh died on April 9, 1978 after having transferred the property to respondents Nos. 2 and 3 in December 1959. In the substitution proceedings, Kathpalia asserted that he first learned of the death through a letter delivered to the Supreme Court Registry on March 2, 1984; the respondents contested that assertion. The judgment also gives inconsistent years for the substitution application, referring in one passage to March 21, 1983 and elsewhere to March 21, 1984. The Supreme Court found sufficient cumulative reasons to condone delay, set aside abatement and permit substitution, but it did not independently establish an undisputed first-knowledge date or reconcile the conflicting filing years.
records.stage: Substitution of deceased respondent and condonation of delay

records.text: The Supreme Court did not finally decide the correct standard-rent amount, the appropriate interim-rent amount, whether subsequently required deposits would be made, or the substantive entitlement to recover possession of the cottage. The historically established deposit of claimed arrears is separate from the future conditional payment duties stated in the remand directions and the analogous precedent. The source-supported judicial holdings and procedural outcomes do not convert unexecuted or UNKNOWN conditional-rule results into TRUE factual premises. Further adjudication remained necessary in the respective remand courts.

In discussing Sections 2(j) and 13(1)(b), the Court explained the statutory significance of unauthorized post-Act subletting, but did not finally adjudicate a separate eviction claim based on unlawful subletting. The judgment records October 10, 1955 in its factual chronology but also reproduces October 1, 1955 when describing the trial court's reasoning. Both stated dates fall within six calendar months of the direct tenancy's effective commencement on May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court expressly held that the application was within time. This statement reports the Court's adopted conclusion; the conflicting filing-date references are not resolved into a single verified date.","status":"SUPREME_COURT_ADOPTED_LIMITATION_HOLDING_WITH_SOURCE_DATE_DISCREPANCY","stage":"Section 8 application and Supreme Court limitation review","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A05","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E03","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E06"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L54","IK-1954254:L55","IK-1954254:L92","IK-1954254:L93","IK-1954254:L106","IK-1954254:L109"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"ISSUING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S06","section":"COUNTERARGUMENT","text":"The District Judge rejected Kathpalia's standard-rent application as time-barred by treating his September 1, 1954 induction as Brook's subtenant, or the earlier letting of the premises, as controlling the limitation period despite his subsequent direct tenancy effective May 1, 1955. The Punjab High Court substantially adopted that interpretation. The Supreme Court expressly rejected their construction of Section 11(b), holding that limitation must be assessed by reference to the relevant letting to the applicant tenant. The lower-court construction is reported solely as a rejected contrary position and is not an operative legal premise.","status":"REPORTED_LOWER_COURT_REASONING_EXPRESSLY_REJECTED_BY_SUPREME_COURT","stage":"District Judge appeal, High Court revision and Supreme Court limitation review","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A04","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A06","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A07","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E04","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E06"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L57","IK-1954254:L58","IK-1954254:L94","IK-1954254:L95","IK-1954254:L101","IK-1954254:L102","IK-1954254:L103","IK-1954254:L104","IK-1954254:L108","IK-1954254:L109"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"HEAD_TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A04"},{"role":"ISSUING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A06"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S07","section":"GROUND","text":"On August 4, 1960, the trial court held Kathpalia's standard-rent application timely and fixed standard rent at Rs. 855 per annum. The District Judge allowed the landlord-side appeal on limitation grounds without deciding the proper amount, and the High Court upheld that limitation approach. Because the amount had not been examined by those appellate courts, the Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971, set aside the adverse limitation decisions, and remitted the landlord's appeal to the District Judge for determination of the proper standard rent. The Supreme Court noted that the claimed arrears had been deposited at the first hearing. This is an actual historical deposit of previously claimed arrears; it does not establish payment of subsequently accruing future rent, compliance with any later valid interim-rent determination, or satisfaction of the separate one-month statutory payment-or-tender condition following a qualifying demand notice.","status":"SUPREME_COURT_RECOUNTED_ACTUAL_DEPOSIT_WITH_LIMITED_LEGAL_EFFECT","stage":"Eviction suit and Section 13(1)(a) payment dispute","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A05","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E01"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L61","IK-1954254:L62","IK-1954254:L72","IK-1954254:L114","IK-1954254:L134"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S10","section":"GROUND","text":"Lakhmir Singh applied on August 1, 1956 for permission to withdraw the arrears deposited by Kathpalia and separately applied on August 27, 1956 under Section 13(5) for directions requiring future rent to be deposited month by month. Kathpalia opposed withdrawal before standard rent had been determined and sought interim-rent determination under Section 9 on October 5, 1956. These applications were procedural requests by the respective parties. Section 4 prevents recovery of rent exceeding standard rent or a lawful increase. Where a standard-rent petition remains pending during an eviction suit based on nonpayment, the trial court should determine standard rent as a preliminary issue or, if that is not practicable, determine interim rent under Section 9 and specify appropriate payment dates and future deposit requirements. An eviction consequence cannot properly rest merely on alleged noncompliance before the required valid determination and directions have been made.","status":"SUPREME_COURT_ADOPTED_STATUTORY_INTERPRETATION_AND_PROCEDURAL_STANDARD","stage":"Supreme Court review of eviction protection and interim rent","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A05","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E07"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L133","IK-1954254:L134","IK-1954254:L135","IK-1954254:L136","IK-1954254:L137","IK-1954254:L138","IK-1954254:L139","IK-1954254:L140","IK-1954254:L143","IK-1954254:L144","IK-1954254:L145"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"ISSUING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S12","section":"COUNTERARGUMENT","text":"In the earlier proceedings, the landlord relied on a purported order dated October 6, 1956 directing Kathpalia to deposit future rent at the agreed monthly rate. The High Court declined relief against the sanction despite having identified serious interpolation in the order record. This describes the historical position adopted in the lower proceedings; it does not establish that the purported direction was genuinely made or legally binding.","status":"REPORTED_LANDLORD_POSITION_TRIAL_COURT_SANCTION_AND_HIGH_COURT_TREATMENT_REJECTED_ON_REVIEW","stage":"Trial court defence sanction and High Court revisions","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A05","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A07"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E05"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L64","IK-1954254:L67","IK-1954254:L68","IK-1954254:L70","IK-1954254:L71","IK-1954254:L119","IK-1954254:L154"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"ISSUING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A05"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S13","section":"GROUND","text":"The original trial record concerning the purported October 6, 1956 rent direction displayed suspicious alterations. The Supreme Court adopted the conclusion that the purported rent direction was interpolated, legally nonexistent and incapable of binding Kathpalia. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Sqfibhai as support for the comparable statutory rent-protection scheme. The cited passage states a conditional sequence: the court first determines standard rent and fixes a date for payment or tender; if the tenant pays or tenders the fixed amount by that date and continues regular payment or tender until final disposition, statutory protection may follow. These are legal conditions drawn from the reported precedent. The passage does not establish that Kathpalia had already fulfilled those conditions or paid future rent.","status":"SUPREME_COURT_REPORTED_ANALOGOUS_PRECEDENT_WITH_CONDITIONAL_PAYMENT_REQUIREMENTS","stage":"Analogous precedent discussed during interim-rent and eviction review","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E07"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L145","IK-1954254:L146","IK-1954254:L147"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S17","section":"GROUND","text":"For Kathpalia's own proceedings, the Supreme Court directed that the trial court first decide the outstanding Section 9 interim-rent application and then call upon the tenant to deposit arrears calculated at the interim rate determined. The District Judge was separately to determine the proper standard rent on remand and call upon the tenant to make good the deposit in accordance with that determination. These are directions establishing a future process and conditional payment obligations; the judgment does not state that those subsequently required payments had already been made.","status":"SUPREME_COURT_ADOPTED_PROSPECTIVE_PROCEDURAL_DIRECTIONS_NOT_ACTUAL_PAYMENT","stage":"Remand directions for interim rent and standard rent","actor_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A03","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A05","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A06","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"],"property_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/P01"],"event_ids":["1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E06","1954254/633f2f3edf116962/E07"],"refs":["IK-1954254:L140","IK-1954254:L144","IK-1954254:L161","IK-1954254:L164","IK-1954254:L165","IK-1954254:L171","IK-1954254:L173"],"role_bindings":[{"role":"TENANT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A01"},{"role":"LANDLORD","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A02"},{"role":"TRANSFEREE","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A03"},{"role":"ISSUING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"},{"role":"REPORTING_COURT","actor_id":"1954254/633f2f3edf116962/A08"}]},{"id":"S18","section":"SUMMARY","text":"The Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971 and remitted the landlord's appeal against the trial court's standard-rent determination to the District Judge, Delhi, for consideration of the proper amount.
