1. A dispute of a trivial nature between a landlord and now his transferees and the tenant is awaiting disposal for over 3 decades thanks to the literal and unimaginative approach to the provisions of a procedural statute which times without number has been described as one for advancing justice and not to make a mockery of it.
IK-1954254:L53
2. A bungalow with an attached cottage situated at No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi was taken on lease by one E. B. Brook and he inducted the appellant as a sub-tenant in the cottage portion which may herein after be referred to as demised premises. Mr. Brook surrendered his tenancy and vacated the portion in his actual possession on April 1, 1955 simultaneously calling upon the appellant to hand over possession of premises in his possession to the then landlord one Lakhmir Singh, who is no more.
IK-1954254:L54
Appellant did not vacate the premises in his possession but reached an agreement with Lakhmir Singh, the then landlord on June 20/22, 1955 to become the direct tenant of the then landlord of the premises in his possession on a monthly rent of Rs. 277.50 p. as stated in plaint, effective from May 1,1955.
IK-1954254:L55
On October 10, 1955 appellant filed a petition in the Court of Senior Sub Judge, Delhi under cite11†Section 8 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 ('Act' for short) praying for determination of the standard rent of the premises effective from the date of the commencement of his tenancy. Landlord Lakhmir Singh entered appearance and contested the application inter-alia contending that the petition was barred by limitation.
IK-1954254:L56
The trial court held that the petition was not barred by limitation and fixed the standard rent at Rs. 855/- p.a. with effect from October 1, 1955. This decision was rendered on Aug. 4, 1960.In the meantime, landlord Lakhmir Singh sold the whole bungalow including the demised premises by a deed of conveyance dated December 21, 1959 in favour of respondents Nos. 2 and 3 who on their own were impleaded in the proceedings.
IK-1954254:L57
3. The original landlord Lakhmir Singh and the two transferees from Lakhmir Singh preferred an appeal against the order of the learned Single Judge determining the standard rent: in the court of the District Judge, Delhi. The learned District Judge was of the opinion that in view of the provision contained in cite12†Section 11(b) the petition filed by the appellant for fixation of standard rent was barred by limitation. Accordingly the appeal was allowed and the petition of the appellant was dismissed.
IK-1954254:L58
4. The appellant preferred Civil Revision No. 335-D of 1961 in the High Court the order of Punjab at Chandigarh against of the learned District Judge. A learned Judge of the High Court agreed with the view taken by the learned District Judge that the petition was barred by limitation and accordingly rejected the civil revision petition by his judgment and order dated December 17, 1962 against which the appellant has preferred Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971 by special leave.
IK-1954254:L59
5. During the pendency of the proceedings for determination of standard rent in the trial court, the then landlord Likhmir Singh filed Civil Suit No. 231/56 in the Court of the Senior Sub Judge, at Delhi on July 3, 1956 against the appellant for recovering the arrears of rent and possession. Eviction was sought under cite13†Section 13(1)(a) of the Act primarily on the ground of default in payment of rent despite notice dated May 10, 1956 having been duly served upon the tenant.
IK-1954254:L60
The appellant as defendant contested the suit inter-alia contending that his petition for fixation of standard rent under cite11†Section 8 of the Act has already been instituted and is pending and unless the standard rent is determined he is not in a position to meet the demand of arrears of rent claimed at the agreed rate.
IK-1954254:L61
It was also contended that a suitable reply stating the afore-mentioned facts to the notice served by the landlord was sent yet he has unnecessarily rushed to the Court without waiting for the determination of standard rent. It appears that alongwith filing of the written statement, the appellant-tenant deposited all the arrears of rent as claimed by the plaintiff-landlord. The then landlord made an application on August 1, 1956 for permission to withdraw the amount of rent deposited by the tenant.
IK-1954254:L62
This application of the landlord was resisted on the ground that the amount has been deposited under protest and the landlord could not be permitted to withdraw the same till the standard rent is determined. The application was set down for hearing on October 1, 1956. In the meantime on August 27, 1956 the landlord filed an application under cite14†Section 13(5) of the Act for a direction that the tenant i should deposit the rent as it falls due month by month.
IK-1954254:L63
The order sheet shows that the Court directed notice of the application to be served upon the tenant and be fixed for hearing on October 1, 1956. It appears that the application for withdrawal of the rent deposited by the tenant was heard on October 1, 1956. On October 5, 1956, '. the appellant tenant moved an application under cite15†Section 9 of the Act for fixing interim rent pending the determination of the standard rent of the premises.
IK-1954254:L64
The order sheet shows that the application was set down for hearing on the same day in the afternoon and it was as a matter of fact heard and adjourned for order to October 5, 1956 in the afternoon. An order purports to have been passed on October 6, 1956 to the effect that the Court directed the tenant to deposit future rent at the agreed rate of rent. The appellant contended that what appears to be the order dated October 6, 1956 is a subsequently interpolated writing and no such order was made.
IK-1954254:L65
It is not necessary to refer to the unsavoury details of this allegation save and except that the two learned Judges of the High Court before whom this matter reached at different stages: Justice Tek Chand and Justice D. Falshaw,; both were satisfied that the trial court appeared to be guilty of interpolation and this finding resulted in withdrawal and transfer of the suit pending before the learned Judge to another Court competent to try the same.
IK-1954254:L66
It appears that at one stage, the suit filed by the landlord was dismissed for default but the same was ultimately restored at the instance of the landlord. When the suit stood transferred to another court pursuant to the order made by Falshaw, J.
IK-1954254:L67
an application was made by the landlord to strike off the defence of the tenant on the ground that he failed to comply with the order made on the application dated August 27, 1956 by the landlord by which a direction was given under cite14†Section 13(5) that the tenant should deposit the rent at agreed rate of rent month to month as it becomes due and payable. It may be recalled that it is in respect of this very order that the allegation of interpolation was made and accepted by the High Court.
IK-1954254:L68
The learned Judge before whom the suit came up for hearing pursuant to the order of transfer made by the High Court by his order dated March 17, 1958 accepted the contention of the landlord and ordered the defence of the tenant to be struck off on the ground that the tenant failed to comply with the directions of the Court made under cite14†Section 13(5) of the Act.
IK-1954254:L69
An appeal preferred by the tenant in the Court of the District Judge was dismissed as being barred by limitation after rejecting the application for condoning the delay, if any.
IK-1954254:L70
The appellant tenant filed two revision petitions in the High Court of Punjab; one against the order of the learned District Judge dismissing the appeal as barred by limitation after refusing to condone the delay in preferring the appeal and the second against the order of the trial court striking off the defence of the tenant on the ground that he failed to deposit the rent for the subsequent period from month to month as directed by the order dated October 6, 1956.
IK-1954254:L71
By a common judgment dated December 17, 1962 the learned Single Judge of the High Court after observing that what purports to be the order dated October 6, 1956 was an interpolated writing for the distinct advantage of the landlord, dismissed both the revision petitions. Hence the tenant has preferred Civil Appeals No. 464-65 of 1971 by special leave.
IK-1954254:L72
6. The mere narration of events leading to the present three appeals would be sufficient to convince even the most callous person that an utterly trivial dispute in which serious allegations of interpolation in the record by the learned trial Judge having been accepted, the tenant is under a threat of eviction on the ground of failure to deposit the rent though all the arrears of rent claimed in the suit was deposited on the 1st day of hearing in the trial court.
IK-1954254:L73
7. To dispose of these three appeals, it is necessary to decide the following questions:
IK-1954254:L74

IK-1954254:L75
> i) Whether the petition for determination of standard rent filed by the tenant under cite11†Section 8 of the Act was barred by limitation?
IK-1954254:L76
> ii) Whether in view of the finding of the two learned Judges of the High Court that -the order purporting to be dated October 6, 1956 on application dated August 21, 1956 was interpolated, the failure of the tenant to comply with the same should have been visited with such a drastic order as striking off the defence?
IK-1954254:L77

IK-1954254:L78
> iii) Whether the tenant has made out sufficient cause for condoning the delay in preferring the appeal against the interpolated order dated October 6, 1956?
IK-1954254:L79
8. We will deal with these questions seriatim.
IK-1954254:L80
9. The first question is whether the application made by the appellant under cite11†Section 8 of the Act was barred by limitation or was within time. cite11†Section 8 prescribes the circumstances in which the Court can fix the standard rent of premises to which the Act applies.
IK-1954254:L81
The Court can determine the standard rent if there is a dispute between landlord and tenant regarding the amount of standard rent payable in respect of premises in accordance with the provisions of the Second Schedule; or where at any time on or after the 2nd day of June, 1944 any premises are first let and the rent at which they are let is, in the opinion of the court unreasonable. cite16†Section 11 prescribes the period of limitation for making an application for fixated of standard rent.
IK-1954254:L82
As it is material for the present purpose it may be extracted. It reads as under :
IK-1954254:L83
> 11. Limitation for applications for fixation of standard rent- Any landlord or tenant may file an application to the court for fixing the standard rent of the premises or for determining the lawful increase of such rent.
IK-1954254:L84

IK-1954254:L85
> (a) in the case of any premises which were let or in which the cause of action for lawful increase of rent arose, before the commencement of this Act, within six months from such commencement.
IK-1954254:L86
> (b) in the case of any premises let after the commencement of this Act, within six months from the date on which it is so let; and
IK-1954254:L87

IK-1954254:L88
> (c) in the case of any premises in which the cause of action for lawful increase of rent arises after the commencement of this Act, within six months from that date.
IK-1954254:L89
Provided that the court may entertain the application after the expiry of the said period of six months if it is satisfied that the applicant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the application in time.
IK-1954254:L90
Reliance is placed by the respondent on cite12†Section 11(b) for contending that the petition for determination of standard rent made by the tenant was barred by limitation. A few facts may be recapitulated to appreciate the contention. One Mr. E.B. Brook had taken on rent whole of the bungalow of which the suit premises a cottage formed part. Appellant was inducted as a sub-tenant on September 1, 1954 1 by the head-tenant.
IK-1954254:L91
The head-tenant surrendered his tenancy and vacated and handed over possession of the portion of premises in his possession on April 1, 1955. Prior thereto he had served a notice on the appellant to vacate the premises in his occupation latest by April 1, 1955. Appellant did not vacate the premises. In June 1955 appellant and the landlord arrived at an agreement Ex. P-2 by which appellant was accepted a direct tenant of the premises in his possession from May 1, 1955 on a monthly rent of Rs. 269. 50 p.
IK-1954254:L92
Appellant paid Rs. 539/- as and by way of rent for the months of May and June, 1955. He moved a petition for determination of standard rent': on October 10, 1955. On these admitted facts the question is whether the application was barred by limitation.
IK-1954254:L93
10. learned trial Judge held that tenancy between the landlord and the tenant commenced from May 1, 1955 and as the application for determining the standard rent has to be made within 6 months from the time the premises are let out to the tenant, the petition filed by the tenant on October 1, 1955 is certainly within time. This reasoning appears to be wholly flawless.
IK-1954254:L94
11. However when the matter was taken in appeal at the instance of the landlord, the learned District Judge held that as the appellant ; was inducted as a sub-tenant on Sept. 1,1954 by the head-tenant Mr. Brook and after Mr.
IK-1954254:L95
Brook surrendered his tenancy the appellant was accepted as a direct tenant effective from May 1, 1955, for the purpose of computing limitation, the tenancy of the appellant could be said to have commenced from September 1, 1954 when he was inducted as a sub-tenant and therefore his petition under cite11†Section 8 filed on October 1, 1955 was beyond the period of 6 months and therefore barred by limitation. We find considerable difficulty in accepting this construction of Sub-clause (b) of cite16†Section 11 .
IK-1954254:L96
12. cite16†Section 11 enables either a landlord or a tenant to make an application to the Court for fixing the standard rent of the premises. Sub-clause (b) provides that such a petition has to be filed within 6 months from the date on which premises have been let if they have been so let after the commencement of the Act. Admittedly, in this case the premises were let after the commencement of the Act.
IK-1954254:L97
When it is said that the premises have been let it only means premises lawfully let by the landlord to the tenant.
IK-1954254:L98
Undoubtedly expression 'tenant' in cite17†Section 2(j) of the Act includes a sub-tenant and other persons as have derived the title under a tenant under the provisions of any law before the commencement of the Act but where the sub-tenant has been inducted after the commencement of the Act which is the situation in the present case, the tenant does not include a sub-tenant because cite18†Section 13(1)(b) removes the protection of a tenant against eviction if after the commencement of the Act he has sub-let or assigned or otherwise parted with possession without obtaining the consent of the landlord in writing.
IK-1954254:L99
Appellant was inducted as a sub-tenant after the commencement of the Act and there is no evidence to show that he was so inducted with the written consent of the landlord. The scheme of the Act prohibits sub-letting, assigning or otherwise parting with possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord in writting. Admitedly, the appellant was inducted as sub-tenant by the head-tenant Mr. Brook. However it is an admitted position that after Mr.
IK-1954254:L100
Brook surrendered his tenancy the sub-tenant was accepted as tenant of the premises by the landlord with effect from May 1, 1955 with some increase in the monthly rent.
IK-1954254:L101
13. As the tenancy commenced in this case after the commencement of the Act, a petition for determining standard rent has to be filed within 6 months from the date on which the premises have been let. The learned District Judge was of the opinion that as standard rent is to be fixed in respect of the premises, limitation for making an application for fixing standard rent has to be made within six months from the date of first letting.
IK-1954254:L102
Fixing of standard rent is, it was said, co-related to premises and not the landlord or the tenant. Accordingly it was held that any subsequent letting would not enable such subsequent tenant to move the petition for determining the standard rent. The expression 'within 6 months from the date on which it is so let' has been construed to mean letting or leasing the premises for the first time to anyone after the commencement of the Act.
IK-1954254:L103
If the construction which found favour with the learned District Judge is to be accepted it would lead to a startling result. The landlord can induct a man of his choice at a fabulous rent as a tenant and such a protege can vacate at any time after 6 months and any subsequent tenant would according to the learned District Judge be wholly disabled from filing the petition for determining the standard rent. Such a construction would defeat the very laudable purpose of the socially beneficial legislation.
IK-1954254:L104
Therefore the expression within 6 months from the date on which it is so let'can mean only, let to that tenant who disputes or desires to dispute the standard rent and move the court for determination of standard rent. The words 'so let' can only mean so let to that tenant after the commencement of the cite19†Rent Act .
IK-1954254:L105
This obvious construction did not find favour with the learned District Judge because according to him if such a construction were to be accepted it would amount to giving the fresh period of limitation to a tenant of the premises on the change of the landlord of the premises. Conversely any subsequent tenant would not be able to move the Court for determination of standard rent. Therefore the approach of the learned District Judge with regard to the construction of Clause (b) does not commend to us.
IK-1954254:L106
The language of Clause (b) is simple and unambiguous. It only means that the tenant to whom the premises have been so let and where the tenancy has commenced after the commencement of the Act, such a tenant can move the petition for determination of standard rent within a period of 6 months from the date of commencement of his tenancy.
IK-1954254:L107
Discernible purpose prescribing the period of limitation is not thwarted by this construction because if the tenant of the premises let out to him wants to question the standard rent he must do it expeditiously within a period of 6 months from commencement of his tenancy failing which he will be debarred from questioning the same.
IK-1954254:L108
14. We have dealt with the view taken by the learned District Judge a little more in detail because the learned Single Judge of the High Court has practically adopted the construction which commended to the learned District Judge. We are therefore unable to accept the construction put by the learned Judge of the High Court on Clause 11(b).
IK-1954254:L109
In our opinion on a proper construction, the petition for determination of standard rent filed by the appellant was within time and the learned District Judge was in error in rejecting the petition on the short ground that it was barred by limitation.
IK-1954254:L110
15. It may be mentioned that the learned trial Judge had determined the standard rent but as neither appellate court nor the High Court dealt with the point we are constrained to remand the matter to the learned District Judge to decide the second point as to what is the standard rent of the suit premises.
IK-1954254:L111
16. In this view of the matter Civil Appeal No. 464/71 must succeed and will have to be allowed and the order of the learned District Judge as well as learned Single Judge of the High Court will have to be set aside.
IK-1954254:L112

IK-1954254:L113
17. Question No. 2 and 3 may be dealt with together. There were two revision petitions before the High Court. They arose in the circumstances which have already been set out.
IK-1954254:L114
18. In the suit filed by the landlord for recovery of rent and possession the tenant while contesting the suit had deposited the rent which was alleged to be in arrears under protest pointing out simultaneously that as he has already moved a petition under cite11†Section 8 of the Act for determination of the standard rent, the same may be decided before the landlord is allowed to withdraw the amount deposited by him.
IK-1954254:L115
In the meantime the landlord moved an application requesting the Court to direct the tenant to deposit the future rent from month to month.
IK-1954254:L116
While contesting this application, the tenant pointed out that his petition for determination of standard rent is awaiting disposal and in order to enable him to comply with the order that may be made for depositing the future rent the Court should either determine the standard rent under cite11†Section 8 or the interim rent under cite15†Section 9 at which he should deposit the future rent.
IK-1954254:L117
19. Now before we deal with these two aspects on merits, a reference to a very unsavoury incident that occurred in the course of proceedings in the trial court which necessitated transfer of the proceedings at the instance of the tenant from one court to another court will have to be made.
IK-1954254:L118
20. It appears that on August 1, 1956 landlord applied to the trial court for withdrawal of the amount of rent deposited by the appellant. That application was contested for the reasons hereinbefore pointed out. On August 27, 1956 the landlord made an application requesting the Court to direct the tenant to deposit the future rent from month to month.
IK-1954254:L119
In respect of the second application, the finding of the High Court is that the tenant was directed to deposit the rent at the agreed rate from month and month, and as he failed to comply with the direction, his defence has been rightly struck off and he is not entitled to any relief at the hands of the Court.
IK-1954254:L120
The allegation of the tenant was that no order was made on his application dated August 27, 1956 and that whatever orders appears thereon was subsequently interpolated by the learned Judge, A transfer application alleging interpolation by the learned trial Judge was moved by the tenant and it is an admitted position that by his order dated August 20, 1957 Falshaw, J.
IK-1954254:L121
directed that the suit be withdrawan from the court before which it was pending and transferred it to another court competent to try the suit and the petition for determination of standard rent. Falshaw, J. in this connection observed as under:
IK-1954254:L122
> These allegations are supported by affidavits of the petitioner and his Counsel Mr. B.S. Sethi, Advocate, and it cannot be denied that on the face of it the orders passed on the application for withdrawal of the sum deposited and the application under cite14†Section 13(5) have a highly suspicious appearance in spite of the denial by the Sub Judge himself of any improper conduct.
IK-1954254:L123
The order on the application for the withdrawal of the amount deposited by the defendant appears to have read in its original form "Present Counsel for the parties. Arguments heard.
IK-1954254:L124
For orders in the afternoon" followed by the initials of the Sub Judge and the date "1-10-56" Tt is quite evidence that after the word "The Naib Nazir to report about deposit by 5-10-56" were added and then alongside the original date "For orders on 6-10-56" have been written the word "orders" being apparently written over the figure " 1 " in the date and underneath the original date where appear the initials of the Sub Judge and the fresh date "5-10-56 Similarly in the order on the respondent's application under cite14†Section 13(5) of the order originally read :
IK-1954254:L125
> Present-Counsel for the parties. Arguments heard. For orders in the afternoon.
IK-1954254:L126

IK-1954254:L127
> followed by the initials and date "1-10-56", and subsequently the word "on 6-10-56" have been added together with "The Naib Nazir to report about deposit by 5-10-56".
IK-1954254:L128
> Nobody has appeared on behalf of the respondent, and in my opinion the circumstances are sufficiently suspicious to justify the apprehensions of the petitioner. I accordingly accept the application and order that the pending proceedings between the parties be transferred to the Court of some other Sub Judge.
IK-1954254:L129
> Two things emerge from this order; one that the landlord did not contest the application for transfer and could not controvert the allegations made by the tenant about interpolation in the record, and secondly the allegations made by the tenant that order was interpolated subsequently was accepted by the learned Judge of the High Court When the matter reached the High Court on second occasion, Tek Chand, J re-examined the allegation of interpolation and agreed with the observations of Falshaw, J.
IK-1954254:L130
The pertinent observation is as under :
IK-1954254:L131
> After having carefully seen original record, the suspicion which was aroused in the mind of Falshaw, J. is further confirmed in my own mind. T am not at all satisfied that the order had not been subsequently interpolated and that the addition has been to the distinct advantage of the landlord.
IK-1954254:L132
21. Is it possible to overlook the injudicious act of the trial court and the disconcerting situation flowing from interpolation of court's record so as to reach the conclusion that the tenant failed to comply with the interpolated directions given by the learned trial Judge so as to deny him the protection of the Act.
IK-1954254:L133
22 At this stage it is better to turn to the scheme of the Act. cite20†Section 13 protects a tenant against eviction: It starts with a non-obstante clause and provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or any contract, no decree or order for the recovery of possession of any promises shall be passed by any court in favour of the landlord against the tenant unless the case is brought within one of the enabling provisions set out in the section.
IK-1954254:L134
One such situation is that the tenant has neither paid nor tendered whole of the arrears of rent within one month of the date on which notice of demand for the arrears of rent has been served on him by the landlord in manner provided in cite21†Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. cite11†Section 8 provides for determination of standard rent.
IK-1954254:L135
cite22†Section 4 clearly places an embargo on the right of the landlord to recover as and by any of rent anything in excess of the standard rent, or any lawful increase that may be claimed in it.
IK-1954254:L136
cite22†Section 4 provides that no tenant shall notwithstanding any agreement to the 1 contrary be liable to pay to his landlord for the occupation of any premises any amount in excess of the standard rent of the premises unless such amount is a lawful increase of the standard rent in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
IK-1954254:L137
Sub-cite23†section 2 provides that any agreement for any payment of rent in excess of the standard rent shall 1 be null and void and shall be construed as if it was an agreement for payment of the standard rent only. Therefore it is indisputable that the tenant is under an obligation to pay standard rent or lawful increase that may be made to it.
IK-1954254:L138
Now where the landlord demands rent at the contractual rate and the tenant has moved a petition for 1 fixation of standard rent how is the tenant to be relieved from the obligation to deposit the agreed rent till the petition for standard rent is decided. To make the scheme of the law effective where the tenant has moved a petition for determination of standard rent, the court must decide it as and by way of a preliminary issue.
IK-1954254:L139
Assuming it is not possible to determine the standard rent as and by way of preliminary issue, the Legislature has taken care to provide for interim arrangement.
IK-1954254:L140
cite15†Section 9 provides that if an application for fixing the standard rent or for determining lawful increase to standard rent is made under cite11†Section 8 , the Court shall as expeditiously as possible make an order specifying the amount or the lawful increase to be paid by the tenant to the landlord pending the final decision of the application and shall appoint a date from which the rent or lawful increase so specified shall be deemed to have effect.
IK-1954254:L141
In this case, the tenant did make an application for fixing the interim rent on Oct. 5, 1956 pen- '. ding the determination of the standard rent in the petition moved by him The order found to be interpolated and hence illegal directed the tenant with effect from October 6, 1956 to pay interim rent at the agreed rate of rent. This order specifying interim rent is found to be interpolated and hence a nullity not binding on the tenant.
IK-1954254:L142
And it is the failure of the tenant to comply with this nullity which has resulted in his defence being struck off. The learned Judge declined to interfere with such an order.
IK-1954254:L143
23 Where the law enables the tenant to move a petition for determination of standard rent and further confers power on the court to determine interim rent so as to enable the tenant to deposit the future rent the failure of the court to give appropriate directions in this behalf would work serious hardship to the tenant more so where the landlord has already filed a suit for eviction on the ground of default in payment of rent.
IK-1954254:L144
In such a situation to give effect to the purpose and object of the Act, the appropriate thing to do would be either to take up the petition for determining the standard rent as a preliminary issue or if it is not possible the court should determine the interim rent fixing a date by which the tenant should deposit the rent in arrears and I direction be given to deposit the future rent at the rate at which interim rent is determined.
IK-1954254:L145
Till these steps are taken and non compliance alleged it would not be open to the court to pass a decree for eviction on the short ground of default in payment of rent. This Legislative scheme clearly emerges from the provisions of the Act and no precedent is necessary to substantiate it. However this Court in cite24†Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v.
IK-1954254:L146
Haji Gulamnabi Haji Sqfibhai after examining the scheme of cite25†Section 12 of the Bombay Rents House and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 which is in pari materia with the scheme of the Act held that where a dispute as to the standard rent is raised and a petition has been filed for determination of the standard rent, and the landlord initiates action for eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent, the court should on the application of the tenant take up the dispute as to standard rent in the first instance and having fixed the standard rent call upon the tenant to pay or tender such standard rent so fixed, on or before a date fixed.
IK-1954254:L147
If the tenant pays the standard rent fixed, on or before the date specified, and continues to pay or tender it regularly till the suit is finally decided, he qualifies for the protection of the Act.
IK-1954254:L148
24. Now reverting to the facts of this case, the landlord applied under cite20†Section 13 for withdrawal of the rent deposited by the tenant. The landlord made another application requesting the court to direct the tenant to pay the future rent at the agreed rate. The landlord then made an application under Sub-cite26†section 5 of cite20†Section 13 to strike off the defence of the tenant on the short ground that the tenant committed default in complying with the direction made by the Court.
IK-1954254:L149
Once it was found that the direction with regard to the payment of future rent at the agreed rate of rent was an inter-polated order, there was no question of complying with such an order, which was legally non-existent. The provisions of Sub-cite26†section 5 of cite20†Section 13 could never have been invoked in the facts and circumstances of this case. Therefore the Court was wholly in error in striking off the defence of the tenant.
IK-1954254:L150
The High Court was clearly in error in upholding such an ; unjust, injudicious and legally non-existent order.
IK-1954254:L151
25. That takes us to the third question. The High Court however experienced one difficulty in granting any relief to the tenant. The tenant had preferred an appeal being Misc. Civil Appeal No. 1 of 1958 against two orders one about the granting permission to withdraw i the amount deposited by him and the second against the interpolated order directing him to pay rent at the rate of Rs. 277. 50 p. per month in future by 10th of every succeeding month.
IK-1954254:L152
When the appeal came up for hearing, it was contended before the learned District Judge, that the appeal was barred by limitation. The tenant had also made an application for condoning the delay. The learned District Judge first examined application for condoning the delay in preferring the appeal and after rejecting the same dismissed the appeal as barred by limitation.
IK-1954254:L153
Two revision petitions were preferred by the tenant in the High Court one against the order refusing to condone the delay and the second against interpolated order and the consequences of its non-compliance.
IK-1954254:L154
26. The High Court first dealing with the view of the learned District Judge that the appeal against the order dated 6th October, 1956 was barred by limitation agreed that the appeal was barred by limitation: and the learned Judge felt constrained in upsetting the finding of the learned District Judge refusing to condone the delay. The learned Judge also therefore declined to give any relief against the order striking off the defence of the tenant.
IK-1954254:L155
27. The history of litigation and the facts set out hereinbefore and the injudicious treatment of the case by the learned trial judge necessitating the transfer was sufficient to interfere with any interim order passed during the proceedings which has a tendency to deny justice. The trial court failed to follow the procedure prescribed by law. On the application for fixing interim relief there is no specific order but there is an interpolated writing.
IK-1954254:L156
Failure to comply with such a honest order had the consequential outcome of striking off the defence. The appeal was not entertained as being barred by limitation. Now if the order dated October 6, 1956 was found to be interpolated how can anyone say with confidence when the record was tempered with by the learned trial Judge. The appeal was preferred on January 2, 1958.
IK-1954254:L157
In the application under cite27†Section 5 of the Limitation Act praying for condoning the delay in preferring the appeal it was specifically stated that the orders under appeal were made in the absence of the appellant and at his back and without communicating the same to him. Further the suit of the respondent landlord was dismissed for default on December 12, 1956 and it was restored to file on December 30, 1957 and within three days thereafter the appeal was preferred.
IK-1954254:L158
Now ordinarily the view of the court dealing with facts in an application under cite27†Section 5 of the Limitation Act would not be interfered unless the failure to exercise jurisdiction would lead to miscarriage of justice. Viewed from this angle the appellant had made out a very convincing and just cause for condoning the delay in preferring the appeal. The order under appeal was the very interpolated order. When was it interpolated? There is no definite answer.
IK-1954254:L159
Within a month and half of the interpolated order, the suit of the landlord was dismissed. Once the suit was dismissed the appellant tenant could not prefer an appeal against an interim order. The suit of the landlord was restored to file on December 30, 1957. Promptly within three days on January 2, 1958 the appeal was preferred with an application for condoning the delay. A just and convincing cause wholly sufficient to condone the delay was thus made out.
IK-1954254:L160
More so because failure of the learned District Judge and the learned Single Judge of the High Court to condone delay resulted in the gross miscarriage of justice in as much as the tenant lost protection of the Act for his failure to comply with a non est injudicious order, which was a nullity in the eye of law. In this background, we find it difficult to uphold the view of the learned District Judge and the High Court.
IK-1954254:L161
28. Justice demands that the order dated October 6, 1956 must be set aside as it is an interpolated and therefore legally non-existant order. It must accordingly be held that the application for fixing interim rent still remains undecided and the trial court will have to decide it as expeditiously as possible.
IK-1954254:L162
If the application for interim rent is not disposed of by an appropriate order there was no question of Won- compliance with the same and therefore no occasion would arise for striking off defence of the tenant. Accordingly the orders dated October 6, 1956 and the order striking off the defence dated March 4, 1958 are set aside.
IK-1954254:L163
The order of the learned District Judge declining to condone the delay in preferring the appeal against the order dated October 6, 1956 is set aside and the order of the High Court disposing of the two revision petitions is also set aside.
IK-1954254:L164
29. Accordingly both these appeals will have to be allowed and the matter will have to be remitted to the trial court for first deciding the application for fixing the interim rent and calling upon the tenant to deposit the interim rent in arrears at the rate of interim rent so fixed. Learned District Judge should take up the appeal against the order determining the standard rent as early as possible and call upon the tenant to make good the deposit in accordance with the standard rent so determined.
IK-1954254:L165
The order striking off the defence is set aside and the tenant will be entitled to defend the suit on merits.
IK-1954254:L166
30. Before we conclude the judgment, one aspect to which our attention was drawn may be noticed. Original landlord Lakhmir Singh died on April 9, 1978 during the pendency of these appeals in this Court. Civil Misc. Petitions No. 17962-69 of 1984 were moved on March 21, 1983 for substitution of his heirs and legal representatives arid for condoning delay, if any, in moving the petitions. The ground on which condonation of delay is sought has been set out in the petition and affidavit in support.
IK-1954254:L167
Appellant has stated in the petition that learned Counsel for respondent Nos. 2 and 3 handed over a letter to the Registry on March 2, 1984 intimating about the death of first respondent, the original landlord. Thereafter the petition for substitution was moved on March 21, 1984 that is within three weeks from the date of the knowledge conveyed by the letter of the learned Counsel for respondents Nos. 2 and 3. The date of death of respondent No.
IK-1954254:L168
1 is not disputed but it is said that appellant came to know about it for the first time from the aforementioned letter. This is countered by the respondents. In our opinion there is good and sufficient reason for condoning delay and granting substitution in the facts of this case. First respondent who is dead was the original landlord and he conveyed and transferred the whole property including the suit premises to respondents No. 2 and 3 way back on December 21, 1959 and since then respondents No.
IK-1954254:L169
2 and 3 are the Veal contesting respondents. Respondent No. 1 has lost all interest if) the property and the litigation concerning the property sold and conveyed by him a quarter of a century back. Coupled with this is the fact that under Rule 10A of Order 22 a duty is cast on the pleader appearing for the deceased party to give intimation of the same to the opposite party.
IK-1954254:L170
This duty in this case was discharged on March 2, 1984 that is six years after the death and promptly within three weeks the petition for substitution is filed. Having regard to the cumulative effect of all these facts we are satisfied that the appellant has made out a sufficient case for condoning the delay in seeking substitution. We accordingly set aside abatement of appeal and grant substitution.
IK-1954254:L171
31. In view of the discussion, C.A. No. 464 of 1971 is allowed and the orders of the District Judge and the High Court are set aside and the matter is remitted to the District Judge for hearing the appeal of the landlord against the decision of the trial court fixing standard rent at Rs. 855/- per annum.
IK-1954254:L172

IK-1954254:L173
32. C. A. No. 465-466 of 1971 are allowed. The matter is remitted to the trial court to dispose of the proceedings on merits in the light of the observations made in the judgment.
IK-1954254:L174
33. In the circumstances of the case parties are left to bear their own costs throughout.

row.description: The cottage portion of No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi, attached to the bungalow
The landlord applied to withdraw the tenant deposited rent and separately sought directions for payment of future rent.
The tenant sought determination of standard rent in October 1955; the judgment describes both 10 October and 1 October as the filing date.
The trial court held the standard-rent petition timely and fixed standard rent at Rs.855 per annum.
The District Judge treated the standard-rent petition as time-barred and allowed the landlord appeal.
The High Court dismissed the revisions concerning refusal to condone delay and striking off the defence despite identifying the purported future-rent order as interpolated.
The Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal 464 of 1971 and remitted to the District Judge the landlord appeal concerning the standard-rent determination.
The Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeals 465-466 of 1971, remitted to the trial court for proceedings on merits, and restored the tenant ability to defend; interim rent remained to be determined.
The tenant asserted first learning of the original landlord death from the March 1984 letter; respondents disputed that claimed knowledge date.

claim.text: The principal dispute concerns O. P. Kathpalia's tenancy and continued possession of the cottage attached to the bungalow at No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi. E. B. Brook originally leased the bungalow and inducted Kathpalia as a subtenant of the cottage. After Brook surrendered his tenancy, the original landlord, Lakhmir Singh, accepted Kathpalia as his direct tenant effective May 1, 1955. Lakhmir Singh subsequently transferred the entire property to respondents Nos. 2 and 3, who became the real contesting respondents. The litigation concerned the timeliness and determination of standard rent, the landlord's claim for arrears and possession, the validity of an alleged future-rent deposit direction, and the tenant's right to defend the possession suit.
claim.stage: Overall tenancy, standard-rent and possession litigation

claim.text: Brook inducted Kathpalia as a subtenant of the cottage on September 1, 1954, after commencement of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952. Brook surrendered his head tenancy on April 1, 1955, but Kathpalia remained in possession. By an agreement reached in June 1955, Lakhmir Singh accepted Kathpalia as a direct tenant effective May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court treated this subsequent direct tenancy as the relevant letting for the limitation dispute.
claim.stage: Tenancy formation and classification for Section 11(b)

claim.text: Under Section 11(b), as construed and adopted by the Supreme Court, the six-month period for a standard-rent application concerning premises let after commencement of the Act runs from the commencement of the relevant letting to the particular applicant tenant. It does not necessarily run from the first-ever letting of the premises or from an earlier subtenancy that preceded recognition of the applicant's direct tenancy. The Court reasoned that the contrary construction would prevent subsequent tenants from challenging unreasonable rent and frustrate the protective purpose of the legislation.
claim.stage: Supreme Court review of Section 11(b) limitation

claim.text: The Supreme Court distinguished Kathpalia's earlier post-Act subtenancy from his subsequently recognized direct tenancy. It observed that the record contained no evidence establishing that Lakhmir Singh had given written consent to Brook's induction of Kathpalia as subtenant. In discussing Sections 2(j) and 13(1)(b), the Court explained the statutory significance of unauthorized post-Act subletting, but did not finally adjudicate a separate eviction claim based on unlawful subletting. The absence of evidence of written consent is an evidentiary assessment, not independent proof that consent could never have existed.
claim.stage: Classification of post-Act subtenancy and direct tenancy

claim.text: Kathpalia filed his Section 8 application for determination of standard rent in October 1955. The judgment records October 10, 1955 in its factual chronology but also reproduces October 1, 1955 when describing the trial court's reasoning. Both stated dates fall within six calendar months of the direct tenancy's effective commencement on May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court expressly held that the application was within time. This statement reports the Court's adopted conclusion; the conflicting filing-date references are not resolved into a single verified date.
claim.stage: Section 8 application and Supreme Court limitation review

claim.text: The District Judge rejected Kathpalia's standard-rent application as time-barred by treating his September 1, 1954 induction as Brook's subtenant, or the earlier letting of the premises, as controlling the limitation period despite his subsequent direct tenancy effective May 1, 1955. The Punjab High Court substantially adopted that interpretation. The Supreme Court expressly rejected their construction of Section 11(b), holding that limitation must be assessed by reference to the relevant letting to the applicant tenant. The lower-court construction is reported solely as a rejected contrary position and is not an operative legal premise.
claim.stage: District Judge appeal, High Court revision and Supreme Court limitation review

claim.text: On August 4, 1960, the trial court held Kathpalia's standard-rent application timely and fixed standard rent at Rs. 855 per annum. The District Judge allowed the landlord-side appeal on limitation grounds without deciding the proper amount, and the High Court upheld that limitation approach. Because the amount had not been examined by those appellate courts, the Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971, set aside the adverse limitation decisions, and remitted the landlord's appeal to the District Judge for determination of the proper standard rent. The Supreme Court did not finally fix or affirm Rs. 855 per annum as the operative standard rent.
claim.stage: Standard-rent determination, Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971

claim.text: Lakhmir Singh commenced Civil Suit No. 231/56 on July 3, 1956, seeking recovery of rent arrears and possession under Section 13(1)(a), alleging default despite a demand notice dated May 10, 1956. Kathpalia disputed the claim, explaining that his standard-rent application was pending and that the claimed arrears were calculated at the disputed contractual rate. The landlord's pleaded nonpayment allegation is not equivalent to a judicial determination that every statutory condition for eviction was satisfied.
claim.stage: Trial court rent recovery and possession suit

claim.text: Kathpalia deposited the arrears of rent claimed by Lakhmir Singh during the trial proceedings, under protest and while maintaining his challenge to the contractual rate. The Supreme Court noted that the claimed arrears had been deposited at the first hearing. This is an actual historical deposit of previously claimed arrears; it does not establish payment of subsequently accruing future rent, compliance with any later valid interim-rent determination, or satisfaction of the separate one-month statutory payment-or-tender condition following a qualifying demand notice.
claim.stage: Eviction suit and Section 13(1)(a) payment dispute

claim.text: Lakhmir Singh applied on August 1, 1956 for permission to withdraw the arrears deposited by Kathpalia and separately applied on August 27, 1956 under Section 13(5) for directions requiring future rent to be deposited month by month. Kathpalia opposed withdrawal before standard rent had been determined and sought interim-rent determination under Section 9 on October 5, 1956. These applications were procedural requests by the respective parties. Filing them did not itself establish an effective future-rent deposit order or actual payment under such an order.
claim.stage: Trial suit rent applications and Section 9 interim-rent request

claim.text: The Supreme Court adopted the statutory reasoning that Section 13 protects a tenant against recovery of possession unless an applicable statutory enabling ground is established. Section 4 prevents recovery of rent exceeding standard rent or a lawful increase. Where a standard-rent petition remains pending during an eviction suit based on nonpayment, the trial court should determine standard rent as a preliminary issue or, if that is not practicable, determine interim rent under Section 9 and specify appropriate payment dates and future deposit requirements. An eviction consequence cannot properly rest merely on alleged noncompliance before the required valid determination and directions have been made.
claim.stage: Supreme Court review of eviction protection and interim rent

claim.text: In the earlier proceedings, the landlord relied on a purported order dated October 6, 1956 directing Kathpalia to deposit future rent at the agreed monthly rate. The trial court subsequently struck off Kathpalia's defence on the asserted ground of noncompliance with that direction. The High Court declined relief against the sanction despite having identified serious interpolation in the order record. This describes the historical position adopted in the lower proceedings; it does not establish that the purported direction was genuinely made or legally binding.
claim.stage: Trial court defence sanction and High Court revisions

claim.text: The original trial record concerning the purported October 6, 1956 rent direction displayed suspicious alterations. Justice Falshaw of the Punjab High Court ordered transfer of the pending proceedings to another competent trial court on August 20, 1957, and Justice Tek Chand subsequently confirmed the concern about interpolation. The Supreme Court adopted the conclusion that the purported rent direction was interpolated, legally nonexistent and incapable of binding Kathpalia. The precise date on which the record was altered was not established.
claim.stage: High Court transfer proceedings and Supreme Court review of interpolated order

claim.text: Because the purported future-rent direction was a legal nullity, the Supreme Court held that failure to comply with it could not justify striking off Kathpalia's defence under Section 13(5). The Court set aside the interpolated order dated October 6, 1956 and the order striking off the defence, and held that Kathpalia must be permitted to defend the possession suit on its merits. This restores procedural protection and an opportunity to contest eviction; it is not a final adjudication that Kathpalia has an unconditional or permanent right to possession.
claim.stage: Civil Appeals Nos. 465 and 466 of 1971, defence sanction review

claim.text: The landlord's suit had been dismissed for default on December 12, 1956 and restored on December 30, 1957. Kathpalia appealed on January 2, 1958 and sought condonation of delay. His assertion that the challenged orders had been made without communication to him was presented in the condonation application, not independently established as an exact notification history. The Supreme Court found sufficient cause for condonation in the procedural chronology, the uncertain timing of the interpolated order and the serious injustice arising from loss of the statutory defence. It set aside the refusal to condone delay and the related High Court orders.
claim.stage: Miscellaneous civil appeal, High Court revisions and Supreme Court delay review

claim.text: The Supreme Court referred to its earlier decision in Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Sqfibhai as support for the comparable statutory rent-protection scheme. The cited passage states a conditional sequence: the court first determines standard rent and fixes a date for payment or tender; if the tenant pays or tenders the fixed amount by that date and continues regular payment or tender until final disposition, statutory protection may follow. These are legal conditions drawn from the reported precedent. The passage does not establish that Kathpalia had already fulfilled those conditions or paid future rent.
claim.stage: Analogous precedent discussed during interim-rent and eviction review

claim.text: For Kathpalia's own proceedings, the Supreme Court directed that the trial court first decide the outstanding Section 9 interim-rent application and then call upon the tenant to deposit arrears calculated at the interim rate determined. The District Judge was separately to determine the proper standard rent on remand and call upon the tenant to make good the deposit in accordance with that determination. These are directions establishing a future process and conditional payment obligations; the judgment does not state that those subsequently required payments had already been made.
claim.stage: Remand directions for interim rent and standard rent

claim.text: The Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971 and remitted the landlord's appeal against the trial court's standard-rent determination to the District Judge, Delhi, for consideration of the proper amount. Separately, it allowed Civil Appeals Nos. 465 and 466 of 1971 and remitted the proceedings concerning interim rent, rent recovery and possession to the trial court for further adjudication on their merits, with Kathpalia's defence restored. The two remands have different receiving courts and different issues. Neither remand constitutes a final determination of the standard-rent amount, an adjudication that all future rent was paid, or a final decision awarding permanent possession to either side.
claim.stage: Final appellate orders and remand scope

claim.text: The judgment contains inconsistent statements about the monthly contractual rent. Its initial account reports Rs. 277.50 per month as stated in the plaint, while its later account of the direct tenancy reports Rs. 269.50 per month and a payment of Rs. 539 for May and June 1955. The earlier purported future-rent order is described using Rs. 277.50. These statements should not be silently reconciled into a single verified contractual amount. The Rs. 855 annual standard rent was fixed at trial level but remained subject to the remitted landlord appeal.
claim.stage: Direct tenancy, contractual rent and standard-rent appeal

claim.text: The judgment expressly identifies October 10, 1955 as the filing date of Kathpalia's standard-rent application in its factual chronology, but reproduces October 1, 1955 in passages describing the trial court's and District Judge's limitation reasoning. The source does not resolve this discrepancy. The Supreme Court's conclusion that the application was timely is a reported judicial holding; the statement pack does not replace the conflicting date references with an independently verified single filing date.
claim.stage: Standard-rent petition and limitation review

claim.text: Lakhmir Singh died on April 9, 1978 after having transferred the property to respondents Nos. 2 and 3 in December 1959. In the substitution proceedings, Kathpalia asserted that he first learned of the death through a letter delivered to the Supreme Court Registry on March 2, 1984; the respondents contested that assertion. The judgment also gives inconsistent years for the substitution application, referring in one passage to March 21, 1983 and elsewhere to March 21, 1984. The Supreme Court found sufficient cumulative reasons to condone delay, set aside abatement and permit substitution, but it did not independently establish an undisputed first-knowledge date or reconcile the conflicting filing years.
claim.stage: Substitution of deceased respondent and condonation of delay

claim.text: The Supreme Court did not finally decide the correct standard-rent amount, the appropriate interim-rent amount, whether subsequently required deposits would be made, or the substantive entitlement to recover possession of the cottage. The historically established deposit of claimed arrears is separate from the future conditional payment duties stated in the remand directions and the analogous precedent. The source-supported judicial holdings and procedural outcomes do not convert unexecuted or UNKNOWN conditional-rule results into TRUE factual premises. Further adjudication remained necessary in the respective remand courts.
claim.stage: Scope of Supreme Court decision and remitted proceedings
